readerTitle: Every café got better. None got ahead.
caseNote: 가상 사례 (점심 식당 거리, 예약 앱) + 실제 연구 (Porter, 1996 'What Is Strategy?')
insight: 남들과 같은 일을 더 잘하는 것은 따라잡히기 마련이고, 남들과 다른 일을 고르는 것만이 앞서 나갈 이유가 된다.
misconception: 더 빠르고 더 싸고 더 잘하면 그게 곧 전략이다. 운영을 개선하면 경쟁에서 이긴다.

sources.text: Porter, M. (1996). What Is Strategy? Harvard Business Review, Nov–Dec 1996.
식당 거리와 예약 앱 사례는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: Porter(1996)가 'operational effectiveness'와 'strategy'를 구분하고 'competitive convergence'라는 표현을 쓴 점을 원문에서 다시 확인하세요.
Porter가 1980년대 일본 제조업체의 품질·비용 우위가 경쟁사의 모방으로 좁혀졌다고 논한 부분('Japanese companies rarely have strategies' 절)을 원문에서 확인하세요. 카드에는 일반적인 표현으로만 적었습니다.
식당 네 곳, 키오스크, 물리치료 클리닉 예약 앱은 모두 가상 사례이며 수치(주문 시간 1분 단축, 로딩 40% 단축, 서버비 절반)는 설명용입니다.

cards.title: Every café got better. None got ahead.
body: Four lunch spots share one busy office street. Over two years, each one adds a tablet ordering kiosk, a loyalty app and a faster grill.
Lines got shorter. Food came out hotter. And none of the four owners earned more than before.

image.label: Four near-identical lunch shops in a row
image.brief: 따뜻한 일러스트. 오피스 거리에 점심 가게 네 곳이 나란히 있고, 네 곳 모두 똑같은 주문 키오스크와 똑같은 메뉴판을 갖춤. 손님 줄은 네 가게에 고르게 나뉨. 실제 브랜드 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Your sales have been flat for a year.
body: You own one of the four lunch spots. A supplier is pitching a new ordering system that cuts each order by about a minute.

options.text: Buy the system. Faster service is what customers notice
options.feedback: You may need it just to keep up. But the other three can buy the same system next month, and then you're back where you started.

options.text: Pick a type of customer the street serves badly, and rebuild your menu, hours and space around them
options.feedback: Slower and harder, and you may lose some current customers. In return, you offer something rivals can't copy by buying a machine.

options.text: Cut prices 10% to pull customers from the others
options.feedback: It may work for a few weeks. Rivals can match a price cut overnight, and then all four earn less.

cards.title: Good decisions, same result.
body: Each upgrade made sense. Kiosks cut wait times. A shared supplier cut food costs. The same popular grain bowl showed up on every menu.
But every shop made the same decisions, so the shops became the same. Customers still split four ways. The gains went to customers, through better service and lower prices, not to the owners.

image.label: Four shops climbing the same ladder side by side
image.brief: 네 가게 주인이 똑같은 사다리를 나란히 오르는 그림. 모두 한 칸씩 올라가지만 서로의 높이 차이는 그대로. 사다리 칸에 "Kiosk", "Loyalty app", "Faster grill" 라벨.

cards.title: Strategy vs efficiency
body: **Efficiency** (Michael Porter called it *operational effectiveness*) means doing the same things as your rivals, but better: faster, cheaper, with fewer mistakes.
**Strategy** means choosing to do different things, or the same things differently, so you offer value rivals don't.
A quick test: if a rival could copy it by buying the same tool or hiring the same consultant, it's efficiency.

image.label: Two paths: same race faster vs a different race
image.brief: 두 갈래 그림. 왼쪽은 모두 같은 트랙을 달리는 주자들("Efficiency: same race, faster"), 오른쪽은 한 주자가 다른 방향의 자기 길로 감("Strategy: a different race"). 깔끔한 인포그래픽 스타일.

cards.title: Best practices spread.
body: Suppliers sell the same equipment to everyone. Staff and consultants carry ideas from one company to the next. So improvements that work get copied.

As rivals copy each other, they drift together. Porter called this **competitive convergence**: companies start to look alike, and competition turns into a race on price. In his 1996 essay, he pointed to Japanese manufacturers of the 1980s, whose lead in quality and cost narrowed as rivals adopted the same methods.

cards.title: Efficiency gets you in. Strategy gets you chosen.
body: Efficiency is not optional. A café with a clever idea and a 20-minute wait still loses. Think of efficiency as the price of entry, and strategy as the reason customers pick you.
The two answer different questions. Efficiency asks, "How do we do this better?" Strategy asks, "What should we do that others don't, and for whom?"
cards.softwareNote: Software makes this sharper. Speed fixes, cloud savings and popular features get copied within months. A product built around one group's specific workflow is much harder to match.

cards.title: Different isn't automatically better.
body: "We have a strategy" is no excuse for sloppy work. And being different only counts if some customers value the difference enough to choose you for it.

The line can also blur. An efficiency edge rivals truly can't copy, like a process refined over many years, can become part of a strategy. The useful question is always: how long before others catch up?

cards.title: Now it's a booking app.
body: You run a scheduling app for small businesses. Three rivals offer nearly the same features at nearly the same price.
Which move is a strategy, not an efficiency gain?

options.text: Cut the app's load time by 40%
options.feedback: Users will like it, and slow apps lose users. But rivals can match it in a quarter, so it keeps you in the race rather than ahead.

options.text: Move to cheaper hosting and halve server costs
options.feedback: Good for margins, but customers see no difference. Pass the savings on as lower prices, and rivals will simply follow.

options.text: Serve only physical therapy clinics, with insurance checks and treatment-plan booking built in
options.feedback: You give up most of the market, and some users will leave. In return, clinics get what general apps don't offer, and copying it means rebuilding the product.

cards.title: Getting better is not the same as getting different.
body: Efficiency keeps you in the game. Strategy gives customers a reason to pick you over everyone who got just as efficient.
**Try it today:** list your last five improvements. Next to each, write whether a rival could copy it within a year. How many are left?
